source.title: How to scale your HEP ML models: A recipe for robust architecture comparisons at scale
source.authors: M. Vigl; N. Pond; J. Barr; A. Froch; Daniel Guest; N. Hartman; Michael Kagan; L. Heinrich

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in high-energy-physics jet-tagging systems, rather than language models, and reports results on compute-optimal loss and allocation, architecture shape, repeated data, and downstream performance.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports hyperparameter calibration, throughput, and cited scaling results. Hyperparameter values used to tune runs and results cited from other work are not rows. Rows below cover reported outcomes on scaling behavior and the claim versions they measure.
record.test_reason: The study measures compute-optimal loss frontiers, N/D allocation, aspect-ratio effects, repeated-data scaling and loss-to-rejection mapping in HEP jet-tagging transformers, plus toy problems. These are new settings, not language models, with their own results on the claim's form. No version is tested on language models, so every verdict is scoped to HEP or toy systems. V1 explicitly names language models and is untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors conclude that hyperparameter transfer removes a bias otherwise absorbed into fitted exponents and floor. Auxiliary objectives lower classification loss and shift the split toward larger models. Fits on smaller datasets can give biased exponents even when curves look like power laws. Under repetition with early stopping, they predict the jointly optimal model size, horizon, learning rate and batch size with an empirical repeat-cost law.
record.recipe_differences: This is a HEP jet-tagging study, not a language-model replication. It uses transformer taggers, cross-entropy classification loss, HEP datasets, tuned training dynamics, and several compute-optimal fitting approaches.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling depends on fitting method (allocation exponents differ across three approaches), dataset size and onset regime, tuning the learning rate and batch size, training objective, input representation, model aspect ratio, and whether data is repeated. The authors also report that fixed learning rates can cause the apparent scaling curve to turn upward.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal learning rate and batch size follow their own power laws in token budget (b*∝T^0.45, η*∝T^0.10), with exponents that depend on the objective.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal training hyperparameters scale predictably with data budget and must be scaled to obtain unbiased scaling laws.

record.problems: The tested system is HEP jet tagging rather than language modeling. The main frontier is still in the scaling regime and too far from its floor for a reliable floor estimate. Some outcomes are presented only in figures; exact values are not stated in the text. The study reports about 97k A100 GPU-hours but does not validate small-run extrapolations against separately trained runs orders of magnitude larger.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every auxiliary-task head or the detailed repeated-data model-size/data-size grid; retained the paper's stated aggregate comparisons and the principal repeated-data effects. Additional fit, hyperparameter, and throughput measurements were omitted where they do not directly measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Not tested at all: no language-model pretraining loss.
There is no quantitative check of small-run fits against separately trained runs orders of magnitude larger. The Fig. 27 projections are not validated.
Language-model allocation and the Kaplan vs Hoffmann discrepancy are not tested directly; Table 4 only cites those values.
Language models, and architecture details other than width/depth aspect ratio.
Image and video models, and fine-tuning or transfer as scaling regimes.
Language-model downstream tasks; the loss-to-rejection projections are not validated at larger compute.
Parameter-counting choices and the original LM disagreement are not tested.

missing.what: With the learning rate tuned once and held fixed, excess loss departs from the tuned power law and turns upward. The authors say this biases exponents and can hide scaling (toy).
A fixed-LR grid on compressed-jet probes refits to a different law, with a floor above the best measured cell; loss gaps of +0.035 to +0.068.
The compute-optimal allocation is not shifted by the input set; the jet-classification-only objective is the outlier, preferring more data.
The four auxiliary-task losses each follow their own compute-optimal envelope toward their own floor.
With tuning and larger datasets, the allocation exponent a≈0.5 replaces Carpe Datum's 0.10; the authors attribute the difference to tuning and data size.

record.verdict_notes: All results are HEP jet tagging or synthetic toys, never language models. Verdicts on V3, V4, V6 and V7 are kept but scoped to these systems; a researcher may prefer to treat them only as V5 (other-modality) evidence. Fixes to the reader's labels: the V7 label had included R4 and R18–R22, which do not show fit-dependence (R18–R22 show near-parallel frontiers); those are dropped. R10–R12 are moved from V7 supports to V7 limits_scope, since the methods largely agree. R1 describes a pre-power-law transient, not a power law.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss in language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study fits and projects scaling curves, but does not validate predictions from small runs against separately trained runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal model and dataset allocation in HEP jet tagging and a toy problem, not language-model allocations or the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison in language models.
Tests transformer width/depth aspect ratio at fixed parameter count in this tagger family; does not test all architecture details or language models.
Tests HEP jet classification, compressed jet representations, input-feature variants, and repeated-data training. Does not test image/video models, fine-tuning or transfer as scaling regimes.
Tests jet-tagging background rejection against classification loss and compute; does not test language-model downstream tasks.

Tests dependence on fitting approach, data onset, training-hyperparameter tuning, objectives, and repeated-data conditions in HEP/toy settings; does not establish which factors explain disagreements between the original language-model studies.
